presentation.title: Composable Architecture for AI Systems: APIs, MCP, Skills, Sub-Agents, and Workflows
presentation.toc: AI is a powerful tool, but it is not the only tool, and most systems worth building are hybrids of AI and non-AI parts. That line between them doesn't sit neatly between domains. It runs inside every domain, and it should move as you learn. This talk looks at the mechanisms for connecting across that line: APIs, MCP, agent skills, and sub-agents, as well as at workflows as a way to move the line itself: when an agent keeps rediscovering the same business process, that process belongs in deterministic execution, not in a prompt. You'll leave knowing which mechanism belongs where, and how to keep shifting work out of AI as your system settles.

presentation.title: Masterclass: Welcome, Introduction, and Logistics
presentation.author: Frank Kilcommins & Erik Wilde
presentation.toc: AI agents are starting to call APIs autonomously, chain services, and generate integrations that were never explicitly designed by developers. Most API ecosystems are not built for this kind of automated usage, which can lead to unpredictable behavior, unsafe workflows, and loss of control. In this hands-on masterclass, you will explore how AI agents interact with APIs and where automation introduces architectural risks, led by two OpenAPI Ambassadors with deep expertise in API design and governance.

ul.li: Head of Enterprise Architecture at Jentic
Governance Board Member at the OpenAPI Initiative
Co-Maintainer of the Arazzo Specification
Ambassador for the OpenAPI Initiative (OAI)

slide.title: What You Will Be Able to Do

ul.li: Design OpenAPI specifications that stay predictable under automated consumption
Apply Overlay rules to enforce governance across specifications
Model multi-API workflows using Arazzo
Design guardrails that control how AI agents interact with APIs
Evaluate whether an existing API ecosystem is ready for AI-driven orchestration
Plan an incremental strategy to improve AI-readiness over time

presentation.author: Erik Wilde
presentation.toc: How AI agents interact with APIs in modern systems: autonomous endpoint calls, service chaining, and generated integrations. Why traditional API governance models break under automated usage, and the architectural risks that follow. Hands-on exercise: map real-world AI interaction patterns onto your own APIs.

ul.li: Agents call endpoints, chain services, and generate integrations nobody explicitly designed for
The API was written for a developer who reads the docs once and remembers
The agent reads the spec every time, and only the spec
Every assumption a human would forgive becomes a failure point
Most API descriptions need quality improvements anyway
Better descriptions benefit everyone, not just AI agents
Complete and meaningful operation summaries
Comprehensive examples for all operations
Clear error handling
Consistent terminology and naming
Good DX is the foundation for good agent experience (AX)
AI agents need information developers don't typically require:
Everything that developers usually just know
Treat every API like an external one for developers with no context
OpenAPI Initiative (OAI) might add AX-specific fields
Until then, leverage description fields strategically

part.title: Four Ways an API Fails an Agent

li.q: Ambiguity forces an agent to guess. Every guess is a potential failure.

ul.li: Missing descriptions, unclear parameter values, inconsistent field types
A human infers from context. An agent has no context beyond the spec.

li.q: If an agent can do it, it will eventually try it.

ul.li: Endpoints that were never meant to be called in sequence, or called at all
An agent doesn't know your intent — only what the spec allows

li.q: What's not there is often more dangerous than what is.

ul.li: No error responses, no pagination, no security scheme
A human asks a colleague. An agent guesses, or fails silently.

li.q: A spec that's hard to govern is a spec that will be misused at scale.

ul.li: Inconsistent naming, mixed conventions, RPC-style endpoints hiding in a resource-based API
One agent misusing this is a bug. A thousand agents is a pattern.
Open book-catalog-raw.openapi.yaml — a first draft, the kind that ships without governance
Use the four lenses to find where it would fail an agent
15 minutes individually, 5 minutes comparing with your neighbor
Worksheet: risk-mapping-worksheet.md

presentation.title: Agent Skills: Introduction
presentation.author: Frank Kilcommins & Erik Wilde
presentation.toc: Agent skills are reusable, versioned instructions that teach an AI agent how to handle a specific task — consistently, without re-prompting. This session covers what skills are, how agents load and use them, how they differ from plain prompts and MCP tools, and why they matter for reproducible and maintainable API governance work. Followed by a live demo of the jentic-api-scorecard skill.

slide.title: Without Skills: Every Session Starts from Scratch

table.style: border-collapse: collapse ; border: 2px solid #000000 ; width : 90% ; margin : 0 5% ;

ul.li: Specific task or goal orientated help in every session
Knowledge already loaded
Same methodology across teammates

Re-explain context at the start of every conversation
Same question, very different answers each run
Knowledge stays with whoever wrote the best prompt
Model updates significantly change behaviour
The LLM is capable, but context management is challenging

part.title: What Skills Are and How They Work

slide.title: A Skill: Teach Once, Benefit Every Time

ul.li: Structured, reusable instructions packaged as a simple folder
Loaded into the agent's context window when relevant - shapes how it thinks and acts
Explicit scope: does one thing, with some guardrails, in a defined way
Versionable artifact like code) - reviewed, shared, and reused across sessions and agents

slide.p: The benefit: instead of re-prompting your process in every conversation, you encode it once and the agent applies it consistently.
Warning: model updates can impact the behavior of skills.

slide.title: Anatomy of a Skill
slide.p: A skill is a folder. The only required file is SKILL.md:
slide.pre: your-skill-name/ ├── SKILL.md # Required: YAML frontmatter + body instructions ├── scripts/ # Optional: executable code (Python, Bash, etc.) ├── references/ # Optional: documentation loaded as needed └── assets/ # Optional: templates, examples, output formats
slide.p: The YAML frontmatter is the trigger. It tells the agent when to activate the skill:
slide.pre: --- name: your-skill-name description: > What the skill does. Use when the user asks to [specific phrases]. --- # Instructions Step 1: ... Step 2: ...

slide.title: How an Agent Uses a Skill: Progressive Disclosure
slide.p: Skills use a three-level loading system that keeps token usage low:

presentation.title: Module 3: Applying Governance with OpenAPI Overlay
presentation.author: Frank Kilcommins
presentation.toc: Enforcing governance at scale with OpenAPI Overlay: consistent policy layers across specifications without modifying the original contracts. Overlay structure and syntax, and rules for security, usage constraints, and compliance. Hands-on exercise: build an Overlay that applies governance policies to an existing API.

slide.title: What is the OpenAPI Overlay Specification?

ul.li: The OpenAPI Overlay Specification defines a way to modify an existing OpenAPI document without changing the original file.
Overlays are separate YAML / JSON documents containing structured actions (add, update, remove) targeting parts of an OpenAPI document.
Targets are identified using JSONPath expressions, enabling precise and repeatable transformations.
The Overlay Specification is an official OAI standard (v1.1.0) designed to support cleaner API workflows and automation.
Overlays allow changes to be applied incrementally, layered, and versioned independently of the base OpenAPI Document.
Separation of concerns: Keep the canonical API definition clean, while applying environment-, audience-, or workflow-specific changes via overlays.
Consistency & automation: Apply repeatable updates across OpenAPI docs (e.g., documentation, metadata, security, examples) without manual editing.
Multi-audience support: Generate public, private, partner, or internal API descriptions from one source using different overlays.
Avoids oversharing: Remove internal endpoints or sensitive fields for public-facing specs without duplicating files.
Integration in pipelines: Overlays can be applied during CI/CD to prepare API definitions for documentation, SDKs, testing, or gateways.
Localization: Translating documentation into another language.
An Overlay document has three top-level fields: overlay (version), info, and actions.
Actions are processed in order, allowing sequential and predictable transformations to the base OpenAPI spec.
Each Action Object contains a target (a JSONPath expression) and an operation such as update, remove, or copy.
Targets can point to any part of the OpenAPI document: paths, operations, parameters, descriptions, vendor extensions, security, metadata, etc.
Overlays are fully valid YAML/JSON documents and can be version-controlled and reused across pipelines.

slide.title: Basic Overlay Example – Updating Descriptions

ul.li: Overlays can enrich generated or minimal OpenAPI specs with documentation.
Example: enhance the API's description field without touching the source OpenAPI Document.
Example Overlay:

slide.pre: overlay: 1.1.0 info: title: Improve API Descriptions version: 0.1.0 actions: - target: "$.info.description" update: description: "Public API for MyService – includes endpoints for books and orders."

ul.li: This updates info.description in the output OpenAPI Document when the overlay is applied.

slide.title: Advanced Overlay Example – Remove Internal Endpoints

ul.li: Overlays can remove elements based on metadata (e.g., internal endpoints marked with x-internal: true).
Useful for creating a public version of an API from an internal canonical OpenAPI Document.
Example Overlay:

slide.pre: overlay: 1.1.0 info: title: Public API Variant version: 1.0.0 actions: - target: "$.paths.*[?(@.x-internal == true)]" remove: true

ul.li: This removes all paths or operations marked as internal from the final OpenAPI Document.
Can be combined with overlays adding public-facing docs, examples, or vendor extensions.
Overlays can now be used to copy elements.
Combined with remove actions, this enables moving elements between different parts of the OpenAPI Document.
Example Overlay:

td.pre: overlay: 1.1.0 openapi: 3.1.0 info: title: Example API version: 1.0.0 paths: /items: get: responses: 200: description: OK /some-items: delete: responses: 200: description: OK

overlay: 1.1.0 info: title: Update the path for an API endpoint version: 1.0.0 actions: - target: '$.paths' update: { "/new-items": {} } - target: '$.paths["/new-items"]' copy: '$.paths["/items"]' - target: '$.paths["/items"]' remove: true description: 'moves the "items" path item to "new-items"'
openapi: 3.1.0 info: title: Example API version: 1.0.0 paths: /new-items: get: responses: 200: description: OK /some-items: delete: responses: 200: description: OK

slide.title: Where Overlays Fit in the API Lifecycle

ul.li: Begin with a canonical OpenAPI Description (often code-generated or design-first).
Apply overlays to inject descriptions, examples, tags, rate limits, or other metadata without altering the base OpenAPI Document.
Use multiple overlays to tailor the API for different audiences: public, partner, internal, or operational.
Generate derived specs during CI/CD for documentation portals, SDK generation, gateways, mocks, or testing tools.
Overlays help maintain a single source of truth while enabling flexible downstream representations.
Overlays can be applied as automated steps during the build or release process.
Ensures documentation, SDKs, and other artifacts are always generated from a validated and enriched spec.
Important for large teams where manual edits would be error-prone or inconsistent.
Overlay application is deterministic: the same overlay + same base OpenAPI Document produces the same result every time.
Ideal for pipelines that produce “public”, “internal”, “sandbox”, or “gateway-ready” specs from one base definition.

slide.title: When to Use Overlays (and When Not To)

ul.li: You maintain a single authoritative OpenAPI Description but need multiple consumer-specific derivatives.
You want to enrich autogenerated OpenAPI Docs with human-friendly descriptions and examples.
You want to strip internal endpoints or sensitive details before publishing publicly.
You want to version documentation changes separately from functional API changes.
The change reflects reality of the core API itself (e.g., adding a real endpoint or schema change).
Your tooling ecosystem does not yet support overlay application.
You have highly dynamic schemas where direct design-first maintenance is preferred.

presentation.title: Module 4: Modeling API Workflows with Arazzo
presentation.author: Frank Kilcommins
presentation.toc: Why deterministic workflows matter when AI agents orchestrate multiple APIs, and how Arazzo models those interactions. Arazzo structure, and how to define safe repeatable multi-step processes across services. Hands-on exercise: design a multi-API workflow with predictable, governed interactions.

ul.li: The Arazzo Specification is a community-driven open specification within the OpenAPI Initiative, a Linux Foundation Project
Arazzo describes an approach to document use-case oriented workflows in a programmatically readable format
A workflow is a series of API calls which when woven together accomplish a specific task or goal or business objective
The human-readable nature improves the ability of API specifications to tell the story of the API(s) in a manner that can improve the consuming developer experience.
The machine-readable nature allows for intent orientated workflows to be discoverable and executable by AI agents, testing tools, documentation tools, and so on!
Deterministic recipes for the use of APIs
Make sense of large unwieldy API description
Bridge the gap where business flows span more than one API description
Living API documentation and improved consumer developer experience (DX)
Assertable business value (machine readable end-to-end test semantics)
Targeted code generation tooling (think SDKs, MCP Servers) for APIs driven by use cases
Improved regulatory checks via assertable workflows
The AI potential for value orientated repeatable interaction with APIs

img.style: float: right ; height : 65% ; margin : 0% 4% 4% 4% ; filter: drop-shadow(0px 0px 10px rgba(0,0,0,0.6)) ;

ul.li: AsyncAPI support
Chained workflow execution
Advanced JSONPath / XPath selector support
OpenAPI 3.2 alignment
Precision improvements:
Full ABNF grammar
Truthy/Falsy condition semantics
And more!
Source Description Object now supports the following document types:
Step Object references operations (or channels) described in AsyncAPI Document using operationId or channelPath.
Async steps define an action (“send” or “receive”) indicating message flow intent.
A correlationId in AsyncAPI links a request with its response, and must be in-sync with the AsyncAPI Document.
A timeout sets the maximum number of milliseconds to wait for the step to complete before aborting and failing the step.
Step Object now has the ability to specify explicit dependencies.
These are a list of steps that MUST be completed before the current step can be executed.
dependsOn only establishes a prerequisite relationship for the current step and does not trigger execution of the referenced steps.
Action Objects now fully support chaining workflows, and mapping workflow inputs using the parameters fixed field.
A new Selector Object which is usable across workflow outputs, step outputs, requestbody payloads, parameter values, payload replacement values.
Enables fine-grained traversal and precise data selection from structured data such as JSON or XML, using a defined selector syntax such as jsonpath, xpath, or jsonpointer.
The context sets the root node for the selector.
The selector specifies the expression.
The type specifies the selector syntax.
Overriding the default Selector Expression versions via the Expression Type Object (renamed from Criterion Expression Type Object)
Specify the type and version for the selector expression to override default
The Parameter Object has a new querystring option for the in fixed field, which treats the entire URL query string as a single value.
To ensure interoperability, when referencing an Arazzo Description by URI, references MUST use the target document’s $self if present.
$self is a URI-reference for the Arazzo Description ensuring portable and unambiguous reference resolution.

Single example fields: example on Parameter, Header, Media Type, Request Body, Response, and JSON Schema objects.
Multiple examples: examples on Parameter, Header, Media Type, and Link to illustrate variations, error cases, and edge conditions.
OpenAPI locations: paths.<path>.<method>.parameters[].example(s), requestBody.content[*].example(s), responses[status].content[*].example(s), components.schemas.*.example.

slide.title: Use RFC 9457 Problem Details for Errors

ul.li: Error Consistency, Security Signalling, AI Error Reasoning
Standard error schema: define a reusable ProblemDetails in components.schemas following RFC 9457 (for example type, title, status, detail, instance, plus extension members).
Error responses: reference the shared schema from responses[4xx/5xx].content['application/problem+json'].schema and optionally the default response.
AI benefit: predictable error shapes make it easier for agents to detect, classify, and recover from failures programmatically.
Foundational Compliance, Agent Usability, Observability
Success responses: use correct 2xx codes: 200 for successful retrieval, 201 for created resources, 202 for accepted/async, 204 for no-content updates or deletes.
Error responses: model common 4xx/5xx codes with schemas: 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 500, ... not just a single generic 200 or 500.
OpenAPI locations: paths.<path>.<method>.responses[status] with appropriate content, schema and examples per status code.

slide.title: You Can’t Improve What You Can’t Measure!
Jentic's API AI-Readiness Framework
slide.p: An open source framework which evaluates APIs across six developer & AI-readiness dimensions

ul.li: Foundational Compliance
Developer Experience (including tooling compatibility)
Agent Experience
Agent Usability
Security
AI Discoverability

slide.title: Foundational Compliance

p.strong: Evaluates if an API is structurally valid, standards-compliance, and parseable by tooling.

What proportion of $ref references successfully resolve

Measures whether the API's underlying data model is coherent enough for automated reasoning (semantic or logical defects that impact reliable interpretation)

slide.title: Developer Experience

p.strong: Assesses clarity, documentation quality, example coverage, and compatibility with developer tooling.

Checks all examples for Schema Conformance (JSON + XML)
Quantifies linguistic clarity of summaries and descriptions. Basically, how easy is it to understand the intent, and the complexity of verbiage.
Presence of meaningful success and error responses across full surface area

slide.title: AI-Readiness & Agent Experience

p.strong: Evaluates where an API gives enough context for AI systems to understand its intent, constraints, and expected behaviours.

Measures presence of concise descriptions across eligible locations
Rewards APIs that model values semantically, not just as loosely typed strings
Evaluate presence and distinctiveness of operationId values

slide.title: Agent Usability

p.strong: Assesses how efficiently agents can navigate, combine, and execute API operations. Measures orchestration safety and agent ergonomics.

Represents alignment with LLM tool-calling expectations

slide.title: Security

p.strong: Assesses if your API protects data, enforces access controls, and follows secure-by-design practices.

Requires HTTPS for externally exposed hosts
Evaluates the protection of PII/sensitive fields
